items.title: In Praise of Unfinished Things
items.tvi: Ca ngợi những điều dang dở
items.text:
There is a particular kind of guilt reserved for the unfinished: the novel abandoned at chapter three, the language course discontinued after a fortnight, the half-painted fence. We are taught, from childhood, that completion is a virtue and quitting a failing of character. Persistence is celebrated in biographies of the eminent; the many projects they quietly dropped along the way rarely merit a mention.
Yet a case can be made that the unfinished deserves rather more respect than it receives. Not every abandoned endeavour represents a lapse of will. Some are discarded precisely because they have served their purpose: the novel that taught its author she preferred essays, the instrument that revealed a love not of playing but of listening. To insist on finishing them regardless is to mistake the form of an activity for its value.
There is, moreover, an economic argument against compulsive completion. Economists speak of the 'sunk cost fallacy' — the tendency to continue investing in something because of what has already been spent, rather than because of what further investment is likely to yield. The reader who ploughs grimly through a tedious book because she has 'already read half' is committing, in miniature, the same error as the government that pours money into a failing project to avoid admitting it was ill-conceived.
None of this is a licence for flightiness. Much that is worthwhile requires enduring long stretches of tedium, and the ability to persevere through them is genuinely valuable. The skill, perhaps, lies in distinguishing between the discomfort that precedes reward and the discomfort that merely prolongs a mistake — a distinction easier to draw in hindsight than at the time, which is precisely why it is so seldom drawn well.

qs.why: “Some are discarded precisely because they have served their purpose.”

items.title: The Tyranny of Metrics
items.tvi: Sự độc đoán của chỉ số
items.text:
Few ideas in modern management have proved as seductive as the notion that whatever matters can be measured, and whatever is measured can be improved. Hospitals are ranked by waiting times, schools by examination results, researchers by citation counts, and employees by an ever-expanding array of 'key performance indicators'. The appeal is understandable: numbers promise objectivity, accountability and a defence against favouritism.
The difficulty, as the economist Charles Goodhart observed, is that when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure. Once people are rewarded or punished according to a number, they inevitably direct their efforts towards the number itself rather than the underlying goal it was meant to reflect. Schools judged on exam pass rates may quietly discourage weaker pupils from sitting exams; hospitals judged on waiting times may reclassify patients to keep the figures down. The metric improves; the reality it was supposed to capture may not.
More insidiously, the activities most easily quantified are not necessarily those of greatest value. The number of patients a doctor sees is simple to count; the quality of reassurance offered to a frightened patient is not. Where only the countable is rewarded, the uncountable tends to wither — not through any deliberate decision, but through the gradual redirection of attention.
None of this amounts to an argument against measurement as such. Data can reveal problems that intuition overlooks, and organisations that refuse to measure anything are hardly models of efficiency. The point is rather that numbers should inform judgement, not replace it. A metric is a tool for asking questions; treated as an answer, it can do considerable harm.

qs.a: People focus on the number rather than the real goal

qs.a: Measurement is useful if it supports judgement
w: Organisations should stop measuring

qs.why: “numbers should inform judgement, not replace it.”

items.title: Nostalgia Reconsidered
items.tvi: Nhìn lại nỗi hoài niệm
items.text:
For much of its history, nostalgia was regarded not as a sentiment but as a disease. The term was coined in 1688 by a Swiss medical student to describe the debilitating homesickness of soldiers serving abroad, whose symptoms were thought to include fever, fainting and, in extreme cases, death. Physicians proposed remedies ranging from leeches to threats, and as late as the American Civil War, army doctors were still diagnosing it.
The modern view is altogether more benign. Over the past two decades, psychologists have amassed evidence that nostalgia, far from being a malady, serves a range of protective functions. People who are prompted to recall fond memories subsequently report feeling more socially connected, more optimistic about the future and more convinced that their lives have meaning. Intriguingly, nostalgia appears to be triggered more often by negative states — loneliness, boredom, even cold — as though the mind reaches for the past to warm the present.
This is not to say that nostalgia is without its hazards. Collective nostalgia, in which groups idealise a shared past, can be readily exploited by those seeking to portray the present as a decline from some lost golden age. Such narratives tend to be selective, smoothing over the hardships and injustices of earlier times while magnifying contemporary grievances.
The distinction, researchers suggest, may lie between nostalgia that looks backward in order to sustain us and nostalgia that looks backward in order to reject the present. The first draws on memory as a resource; the second treats it as a refuge. Both are recognisably human, but only one tends to leave us better equipped for the life we actually have.

items.title: The Craft of Silence in Fiction
items.tvi: Nghệ thuật im lặng trong tiểu thuyết
items.text:
Among the hardest lessons for apprentice novelists is that what a story leaves unsaid can matter more than what it states. Ernest Hemingway famously likened his method to an iceberg: only a fraction of the meaning should appear on the surface, with the remainder implied by what lies beneath. A writer who knows something deeply, he argued, may omit it, and the reader will sense its presence more strongly than if it had been spelled out.
The principle is easier to admire than to apply. Omission, handled clumsily, produces not resonance but confusion; the reader cannot feel the weight of what has been withheld unless the visible part of the story has been shaped to suggest it. A conversation in which two characters discuss the weather while avoiding any mention of a recent bereavement works only if the reader already knows of the death, or can infer it from the strained politeness of their exchange.
Vietnamese literature offers its own tradition of restraint. Classical poetry frequently conveys grief or longing through images of landscape — a solitary crane, an autumn moon — rather than direct statement, trusting the reader to supply the emotion. Contemporary writers such as Nguyen Huy Thiep have been praised for a spare, almost laconic style in which brutal events are recounted in a flat tone that heightens rather than diminishes their impact.
What these approaches share is a form of respect for the reader. To explain everything is, in a sense, to distrust one's audience. To leave room for inference is to invite them into the act of creation — an invitation that, when it succeeds, produces the peculiar intimacy that distinguishes literature from mere information.

w: Stories should be cold and unemotional

qs.why: “only a fraction of the meaning should appear on the surface, with the remainder implied.”

qs.a: When the story does not give enough clues
w: When the story is too short

qs.why: “the reader cannot feel the weight of what has been withheld unless the visible part… has been shaped to suggest it.”

qs.q: How does classical Vietnamese poetry express emotion?

qs.why: “conveys grief or longing through images of landscape… rather than direct statement.”

w: Readers dislike long books

qs.why: “To explain everything is, in a sense, to distrust one's audience.”

items.title: Expertise and Its Discontents
items.tvi: Chuyên gia và những bất mãn
items.text:
It has become commonplace to lament a crisis of trust in expertise. Scientists, economists and medical professionals, the argument runs, are increasingly dismissed by a public that prefers the confident pronouncements of online commentators to the hedged conclusions of those who have devoted their lives to a subject. There is truth in this, but the diagnosis is often incomplete.
Part of the problem lies with the experts themselves. Forecasts confidently issued and spectacularly wrong — of financial stability on the eve of crisis, for instance — have understandably eroded public faith. So, too, has a tendency in some quarters to present contested findings as settled consensus, or to stray from areas of genuine competence into political advocacy while retaining the authority of the laboratory or the university.
There is also a structural difficulty. Genuine expertise is characterised by an awareness of uncertainty: the specialist knows how much remains unknown and qualifies her statements accordingly. Yet public debate rewards certainty. A commentator who declares that a policy will 'definitely' succeed is likely to attract more attention than one who explains that the evidence is mixed, even though the latter is giving a more accurate picture.
Restoring trust, then, may require changes on both sides. Experts might be more candid about the limits of their knowledge and more careful to distinguish evidence from opinion. The public, for its part, might learn to regard expressions of uncertainty not as weakness but as a mark of honesty. Neither change is easy; but the alternative — a debate in which confidence is mistaken for competence — is considerably worse.

qs.why: “regard expressions of uncertainty not as weakness but as a mark of honesty.”

items.title: The Language of Food
items.tvi: Ngôn ngữ của món ăn
items.text:
Menus are rarely read as literature, yet they repay close attention. Linguists who have analysed thousands of restaurant menus have found that the vocabulary used to describe dishes correlates remarkably closely with their price. Inexpensive establishments tend to rely on vague positive adjectives — 'delicious', 'tasty', 'mouth-watering' — whose very insistence betrays a certain anxiety. Expensive restaurants, by contrast, favour precise, often unadorned detail: the provenance of an ingredient, the name of a farm, a cooking technique stated without embellishment.
The pattern, researchers suggest, reflects different strategies of persuasion. Where quality cannot be taken for granted, it must be asserted; where it can, assertion would seem faintly vulgar, and the restaurant signals confidence through restraint. In one study, every additional letter in the average length of the words describing a dish was associated with a measurable increase in its price — a finding that says less about spelling than about the cultural capital attached to elaborate, often French-derived terminology.
The language of food also carries traces of history. English distinguishes between the animal in the field — cow, pig, sheep — and its meat on the table — beef, pork, mutton — a division usually traced to the Norman conquest, when Anglo-Saxon peasants tended the livestock while their French-speaking lords consumed it. Vietnamese culinary vocabulary, similarly, bears the imprint of contact with Chinese and French cuisine, from 'xì dầu' to 'pa tê'.
To read a menu attentively, then, is to read a compressed account of social class, commerce and history — served, as it were, with a side of persuasion.

items.title: The Paradox of Choice
items.tvi: Nghịch lý của sự lựa chọn
items.text:
It seems self-evident that more choice is better. A shop offering fifty varieties of jam ought to satisfy more customers than one offering five; a pension scheme with a hundred investment options ought to suit more people than one with ten. Yet a body of research, popularised as 'the paradox of choice', suggests that beyond a certain point additional options can leave us less satisfied rather than more.
In a widely cited experiment, shoppers presented with a display of twenty-four jams were more likely to stop and look than those shown only six, but considerably less likely to buy. Faced with abundance, many deferred the decision altogether. Similar effects have been reported in contexts as varied as retirement savings, where larger menus of funds are associated with lower participation, and online dating, where an apparently limitless pool of partners may foster a reluctance to commit to any one of them.
The mechanisms proposed are several. Extensive choice increases the cognitive effort required to decide, and with it the temptation to postpone. It also raises expectations — surely, among so many options, one must be perfect — and multiplies the opportunities for regret, since every choice made implies alternatives forgone.
It should be said that subsequent attempts to replicate the original findings have produced inconsistent results, and the effect appears to depend heavily on context: experts choosing within their own field, for example, seem largely immune. Still, the broader insight endures. Freedom of choice is undoubtedly valuable, but the assumption that its value increases without limit deserves rather more scepticism than it usually receives.

qs.why: “every choice made implies alternatives forgone.”

qs.a: Later studies have not always produced the same results

qs.why: “subsequent attempts to replicate the original findings have produced inconsistent results.”

qs.q: What is the writer's conclusion?
qs.a: Choice is valuable, but not without limit
w: Shops should offer fewer products

qs.why: “the assumption that its value increases without limit deserves rather more scepticism.”

items.title: Monuments and Memory
items.tvi: Tượng đài và ký ức
items.text:
Public monuments occupy a peculiar position in the life of a city. Commissioned to commemorate a particular person or event, they are intended to fix a meaning in bronze or stone for all time. Yet the societies that surround them continue to change, and a statue erected in a spirit of celebration may, a century later, provoke embarrassment, anger or simple indifference.
Recent controversies over the removal of statues in various countries have exposed sharply divergent views of what monuments are for. To some, they are historical documents: to remove them is to erase the past, however uncomfortable, and to deprive future generations of the opportunity to learn from it. To others, this argument confuses history with honour. A statue on a pedestal in a public square, they point out, is not a neutral record but a statement of esteem; history is preserved in archives, museums and textbooks, not in the decision to continue celebrating particular figures.
Between these positions lie a range of compromises. Some cities have added explanatory plaques that place a monument in its historical context; others have relocated contested statues to museums, where they can be displayed alongside critical interpretation. A few have commissioned new works that respond directly to the old, creating a dialogue across time.
What the debate makes clear is that monuments are less about the past than about the present. They tell us not so much what happened as what a community, at a given moment, chooses to honour — and the question of whether that choice still holds is one that each generation is entitled to ask afresh.

items.title: The Uses of Doubt
items.tvi: Lợi ích của sự hoài nghi
items.text:
In most professional settings, doubt is something to be concealed. The confident manager, the decisive surgeon, the barrister who never hesitates — these are the figures we are taught to admire, and admitting uncertainty can feel like admitting incompetence. Yet some of the most consequential errors in history have stemmed not from too much doubt but from too little.
Psychologists have long documented the phenomenon of overconfidence: the tendency to overestimate the accuracy of one's own judgements. In studies where participants are asked to give ranges within which they are ninety percent sure a figure lies, the true answer falls outside those ranges far more often than ten percent of the time. Experts are not immune; in some fields, greater experience appears to increase confidence faster than it increases accuracy.
Certain professions have responded by institutionalising doubt. Aviation and, increasingly, medicine use checklists and procedures that oblige even senior practitioners to verify their assumptions. Some organisations conduct 'pre-mortems', in which a team imagines that a project has already failed and works backwards to identify why — an exercise that legitimises the expression of concerns that hierarchy might otherwise suppress.
The aim is not paralysis. A surgeon who doubted every incision could not operate, and a leader incapable of decision would be no leader at all. The skill lies in locating doubt in the right place: before commitment rather than during execution, and directed at one's own reasoning rather than dispersed as general anxiety. Doubt, so understood, is not the opposite of confidence but its necessary companion — the discipline that keeps confidence honest.

w: People were usually correct

items.title: Walking the City
items.tvi: Đi bộ trong thành phố
items.text:
The nineteenth-century French poet Charles Baudelaire celebrated the flâneur: the idle stroller who wanders the city without purpose, observing its crowds with a detached and curious eye. For Baudelaire, the flâneur was a kind of artist, extracting poetry from the apparently mundane spectacle of urban life. The figure has since become a fixture of literary and cultural criticism, invoked whenever writers wish to describe a particular quality of attention.
It is worth asking, however, who was free to wander in this way. The classic flâneur was male, reasonably affluent and unencumbered by work; a woman walking alone in nineteenth-century Paris risked being taken for a prostitute, and a labourer had neither the time nor the leisure. The supposedly universal experience of the city was, in practice, available to a narrow few.
Contemporary writers have sought to reclaim the practice for a wider constituency. Some have written of the 'flâneuse', the female walker whose movement through the city is itself a quiet assertion of the right to public space. Others have pointed to the ways in which ordinary walking — to work, to market, to school — produces its own forms of knowledge, intimate and unglamorous, about how a city actually functions.
In cities where the car dominates and pavements are an afterthought, the simple act of walking can take on an almost political dimension. To walk is to experience the city at human scale, to notice what speed obscures, and to insist, however implicitly, that streets exist for people rather than merely for traffic. Baudelaire's stroller may have been a privileged figure, but the attention he embodied is available to anyone willing to slow down.

items.title: The Tyranny of Choice
items.tvi: Khi nhiều lựa chọn thành gánh nặng
items.text:
It has become something of an article of faith in affluent societies that choice is an unqualified good. More options, the reasoning goes, mean a better chance of finding precisely what one wants, and the freedom to choose is itself a mark of autonomy. Supermarkets stock dozens of varieties of olive oil; streaming services offer thousands of films; even pension plans arrive with a bewildering menu of funds. Yet a body of research that emerged at the turn of the century has complicated this cheerful picture, suggesting that beyond a certain point, abundance may undermine rather than enhance satisfaction.
The most frequently cited study involved a display of jams in an upmarket grocery store. When shoppers were offered twenty-four varieties, more of them stopped to taste, but far fewer went on to buy than when the selection was limited to six. The researchers interpreted this as evidence of "choice overload": confronted with too many alternatives, people become paralysed, postpone decisions or, having chosen, are tormented by the suspicion that another option would have been better.
It would be convenient if the story ended there, but it does not. Subsequent attempts to replicate the effect have produced inconsistent results, and a large analysis combining dozens of experiments concluded that, on average, the effect of choice overload was close to zero. What appears to matter is context. Overload is more likely when options are difficult to compare, when people have no clear preferences, and when the decision feels consequential. When shoppers know exactly what they want, a large assortment may be helpful rather than harmful.
This more nuanced account has practical implications. Rather than simply reducing the number of options, designers of choices, whether retailers, employers or governments, can make comparison easier by grouping alternatives, highlighting relevant features or offering sensible defaults. The automatic enrolment of employees in pension schemes, with the option to leave, has dramatically increased participation in several countries without restricting anyone's freedom.
The debate also reveals something about the way popular science travels. The jam experiment acquired the status of a parable, retold in books and lectures as if it settled the matter, while the less memorable studies that complicated it received far less attention. A tidy story about the burden of choice proved more appealing than the untidy truth that its effects depend on circumstances. In that sense, the history of the idea is itself a lesson in the dangers of accepting an attractive conclusion without asking how much evidence supports it.

items.title: In Defence of the Unfinished
items.tvi: Biện hộ cho những điều dang dở
items.text:
Every writer I know has a drawer, real or digital, full of abandoned work: novels that stalled at chapter four, essays that lost their argument halfway through, poems that never found their final line. For most of my career I regarded mine with a kind of low-level shame, as a record of failures I preferred not to examine. Lately I have begun to see it differently.
The culture of productivity in which many of us now work tends to treat unfinished projects as waste. Time management advice urges us to complete what we start, to avoid the guilt of loose ends, and to measure our worth by visible output. There is wisdom in this, up to a point. A writer who never finishes anything is unlikely to sustain a career, and perfectionism can be a sophisticated form of avoidance.
But the logic of completion overlooks the way creative work actually develops. Many of the pieces I eventually published began as fragments of earlier abandoned projects: a character who outlived the novel she was created for, a paragraph that only made sense when transplanted into a different essay years later. The drawer, it turns out, was less a graveyard than a seed bank. What looked like waste was in fact a store of possibilities that needed time, and sometimes a different context, to become useful.
There is also something to be said for the experience of stopping. Abandoning a project is rarely a single decision; more often it is a gradual recognition that the work is not going where one hoped, or that one is no longer the person who began it. Acknowledging that honestly, rather than forcing a conclusion, can be an act of judgement rather than weakness. Some of the most disappointing books I have read bear the marks of authors who finished them out of obligation.
None of this is an argument for never finishing anything. Deadlines exist, editors need manuscripts and readers deserve completed books. It is, rather, a plea for a more generous view of what counts as productive. Not every hour of creative effort will result in a finished object, and the hours that do not are not necessarily wasted. The unfinished piece in the drawer may simply be waiting, as many of mine turned out to be, for the moment when its writer has learned enough to complete it.

items.title: The Ethics of Predicting Crime
items.tvi: Đạo đức của việc dự đoán tội phạm
items.text:
Predictive policing, the use of data and algorithms to anticipate where crimes are likely to occur or who is likely to commit them, has been promoted as a way of making law enforcement both more efficient and more objective. If historical patterns can reveal where burglaries cluster or which streets see repeated violence, the argument runs, limited police resources can be deployed where they will do the most good. And because decisions are guided by numbers rather than hunches, they should be less susceptible to individual prejudice.
The difficulty lies in the data on which such systems depend. Records of crime are not a neutral reflection of where crime happens; they are a record of where crime has been detected and reported. If certain neighbourhoods have historically been patrolled more heavily, more offences will have been recorded there, and an algorithm trained on those records will direct still more officers to the same places. The result can be a feedback loop in which past patterns of enforcement are mistaken for patterns of criminal behaviour, and the appearance of objectivity lends them new authority.
Critics also question systems that assess individuals rather than locations. Tools that assign risk scores to people based on factors such as previous arrests, age or associations may reinforce existing inequalities, and those affected often have no means of understanding, let alone challenging, how their score was calculated. When the logic of a system is hidden, whether for commercial reasons or because of its technical complexity, the principle that people should be able to contest decisions made about them is weakened.
Defenders of the technology respond that human judgement is hardly free of bias either, and that a well-designed system can be audited in ways that an individual officer's intuition cannot. Some police forces have published the methods behind their tools and invited independent review, and a few have abandoned programmes that failed to show clear benefits.
The more fundamental question may be what such systems are for. Prediction can inform prevention as well as enforcement: identifying areas at risk might lead to better street lighting, youth services or support for victims rather than simply more arrests. Whether predictive tools contribute to fairer and safer communities may depend less on the sophistication of their algorithms than on the choices made about how their predictions are used.

items.title: Translating Humour
items.tvi: Dịch tiếng cười
items.text:
Translators often say that the hardest thing to carry from one language to another is not poetry or legal terminology but a joke. Puns depend on accidents of sound that rarely survive the crossing; references to local politicians or television programmes mean nothing to foreign readers; and the timing of comic dialogue is bound up with the rhythm of a particular language. A line that provokes laughter in Hanoi may produce only polite confusion in London.
Faced with this difficulty, translators adopt a range of strategies, none of them entirely satisfactory. One is to translate literally and add a footnote explaining why the original was funny, an approach that preserves accuracy at the cost of the humour itself, since few things are less amusing than an explained joke. Another is to replace the original joke with a different one that works in the target language, sacrificing fidelity to the words in order to remain faithful to the effect. A third, more cautious option is simply to omit what cannot be translated, quietly smoothing the text into something less playful than its author intended.
Each choice reflects a view about what translation is for. Those who favour substitution argue that a comic novel exists to make its readers laugh, and that a translation which produces no laughter has failed, however accurate it may be. Their opponents worry that substitution gives translators too much licence, turning them into co-authors who impose their own sense of humour on someone else's work. Readers, for their part, are rarely aware of these decisions, and may judge an author as witty or dull on the basis of choices made by someone whose name appears in small print on the title page.
The problem is not only linguistic but cultural. What people find funny is shaped by shared assumptions about status, politeness and taboo, and humour that relies on gently mocking authority, for instance, may read very differently in societies with different attitudes to hierarchy. A skilled translator must therefore judge not only whether a joke can be rendered in another language but whether its target audience will recognise it as a joke at all.
Perhaps for this reason, comic writing is often among the last to be translated, and some of the funniest books in any language remain largely unknown abroad. It is a loss that goes beyond entertainment: humour reveals a great deal about the way a society sees itself, and a culture known to outsiders only through its serious literature is known only in part.

qs.why: “humour reveals a great deal about the way a society sees itself.”

items.title: The Architecture of Memory
items.tvi: Kiến trúc của ký ức
items.text:
Cities are full of buildings whose original purpose has long since disappeared: factories turned into galleries, railway stations converted into museums, prisons reborn as hotels. Such transformations are usually celebrated as examples of sustainable development, since reusing an existing structure generally consumes far less energy than demolishing it and building anew. But the question of what to keep and what to replace is rarely only technical or economic. It is also a question about collective memory, and about whose past a city chooses to remember.
Architectural conservation has historically favoured the grand and the beautiful. Palaces, cathedrals and the homes of the wealthy were protected, while the ordinary buildings in which most people lived and worked were demolished with little debate. The result is a selective record of the past, one in which the lives of the majority are largely invisible. In recent decades, some conservationists have argued for a broader approach, seeking to preserve working-class housing, markets and industrial sites as evidence of everyday history.
This expansion has its own complications. Once a neighbourhood is designated as historically significant, property values often rise, and the communities whose history is being preserved may find themselves unable to afford to stay. The physical fabric of the past survives while the people who gave it meaning are displaced, leaving behind what critics describe as a stage set: authentic in appearance, emptied of the life it was meant to commemorate.
There are also buildings associated with painful histories, such as former detention centres or sites of political violence. Some argue that these should be preserved precisely because they are uncomfortable, as a means of ensuring that the events they witnessed are not forgotten. Others, often including those directly affected, may prefer that such places be removed or transformed, so that they no longer dominate the landscape of daily life. There is no formula for resolving such disagreements, and decisions made in one generation may be regretted by the next.
What these debates share is a recognition that buildings are never merely buildings. They shape and are shaped by the stories a society tells about itself. Deciding which structures to preserve is therefore a way of deciding which stories will remain visible, and the most thoughtful approaches to conservation are those that involve the people whose memories are at stake.

qs.a: One that includes the people whose memories are involved
w: One led only by architects

qs.why: “the most thoughtful approaches… involve the people whose memories are at stake.”

items.title: The Myth of the Lone Genius
items.tvi: Huyền thoại thiên tài đơn độc
items.text:
Popular histories of science and art are fond of a particular image: the solitary genius, struck by inspiration in a garden or a bath, who single-handedly transforms our understanding of the world. The image is seductive, not least because it flatters our sense that greatness is a property of individuals. It is also, for the most part, misleading.
Closer examination of almost any celebrated breakthrough reveals a crowded scene. Newton's remark about standing on the shoulders of giants may have been partly a barbed joke at a rival's expense, but it was apt nonetheless: his work drew on decades of calculation by others. Darwin corresponded with hundreds of naturalists, breeders and collectors, and was prompted to publish only when a younger naturalist, Alfred Russel Wallace, arrived independently at much the same theory. Simultaneous discovery of this kind is so common that some historians regard it as the norm rather than the exception – a sign that ideas emerge when the conditions for them are ripe.
Why, then, does the myth persist? Partly because stories require protagonists, and a single name is easier to remember than a network. Partly, too, because institutions reward individuals: prizes are awarded to people, not to the conversations that shaped them.
The cost of the myth is not merely historical inaccuracy. Students who believe that real achievement springs from solitary brilliance may conclude, on finding that they need help, that they lack the gift altogether. A more truthful account – of genius as something that happens between people as much as within them – might prove both more accurate and more encouraging.

w: It is supported by most historical evidence
It encourages students to work harder
qs.why: “it flatters our sense that greatness is a property of individuals.”

qs.a: As an example of two people reaching the same idea independently
w: To show that Darwin copied a younger scientist
To prove that Darwin worked entirely alone
qs.why: “arrived independently at much the same theory. Simultaneous discovery of this kind is so common…”

They may copy the work of others
qs.why: “may conclude, on finding that they need help, that they lack the gift altogether.”

items.title: On Apology
items.tvi: Bàn về lời xin lỗi
items.text:
Few public rituals are as closely scrutinised, or as frequently botched, as the apology. A company whose product has harmed customers, a politician caught in an indiscretion, a celebrity whose old remarks have resurfaced: each is expected to say sorry, and each is judged less on whether they do so than on how.
The most common failure is the conditional apology – 'I'm sorry if anyone was offended' – which manages to express regret while locating the problem in the sensitivity of the listener. Close behind is the passive construction, in which 'mistakes were made', as though by no one in particular. Both are attempts to secure the social benefits of contrition without paying its price, which is the acknowledgement of responsibility.
Research on apologies suggests that what people want is surprisingly consistent: a clear statement of what was done wrong, an acceptance of responsibility, an explanation that does not shade into excuse, and some offer of repair. Of these, the acceptance of responsibility appears to matter most; an apology that is eloquent but evasive can be received worse than none at all.
Yet there is a tension here. Lawyers frequently advise clients against apologising, fearing that an admission of fault will be used against them in court. Some jurisdictions have responded with so-called 'apology laws', which prevent expressions of sympathy from being treated as evidence of liability. Whether such laws produce more sincere apologies, or merely more carefully worded ones, remains an open question.

w: It is too long and formal
It promises more than it can deliver
qs.why: “locating the problem in the sensitivity of the listener.”

qs.q: What do the conditional and the passive apology have in common?
qs.a: Both avoid accepting responsibility
w: Both are recommended by lawyers
Both offer to repair the damage
qs.why: “without paying its price, which is the acknowledgement of responsibility.”

qs.q: Which element of an apology seems to matter most?
qs.a: Accepting responsibility
w: Explaining the reasons
Offering compensation
qs.why: “the acceptance of responsibility appears to matter most”

qs.q: What is the writer's attitude to 'apology laws'?
qs.a: Unsure whether they make apologies more sincere
w: Strongly in favour of them
Convinced that they encourage dishonesty
qs.why: “Whether such laws produce more sincere apologies… remains an open question.”

items.title: What Maps Leave Out
items.tvi: Những gì bản đồ bỏ qua
items.text:
We tend to treat maps as neutral pictures of the world, as if the only question to ask of them were whether they are accurate. Yet every map is an argument. To make one, a cartographer must decide what to include and what to omit, which names to use, where to put the centre and how to flatten a curved surface onto a flat page – and each decision shapes what the reader sees.
The most famous example is the Mercator projection, designed in the sixteenth century for navigation. Because it preserves the angles sailors needed for plotting a course, it distorts size, enlarging regions far from the equator: Greenland appears roughly as large as Africa, though Africa is about fourteen times bigger. For centuries this was the image of the world that hung in classrooms, and critics have long argued that it subtly inflated the importance of Europe and North America.
Omission can be as telling as distortion. Colonial maps routinely labelled inhabited regions as empty, a convention that made their seizure easier to justify. Even today, digital maps tend to show in rich detail the streets where businesses cluster, while an informal settlement housing thousands of people may barely register.
None of this means that maps are lies. It means that they are tools, made by particular people for particular purposes. The sensible response is not to distrust every map, but to ask of each one the questions we would ask of any other text: who made this, for whom, and what did they choose to leave out?

items.title: The Right to Be Forgotten
items.tvi: Quyền được lãng quên trên mạng
items.text:
For most of human history, forgetting was the default and remembering required effort. Records decayed, gossip faded, and a youthful mistake could, in time, be outlived. The internet has reversed this arrangement. A careless remark, an unflattering photograph or a newspaper report of a minor offence may now remain searchable for decades, attached to a person's name long after the circumstances have changed.
It was against this background that, in 2014, the European Union's highest court ruled that individuals could, in certain circumstances, ask search engines to remove links to information about them that was 'inadequate, irrelevant or no longer relevant'. The information itself was not deleted; it simply became harder to find by searching a name.
Supporters regard the ruling as a humane recognition that people change, and that a society which never lets anyone escape their past is a harsher one. Critics – among them many journalists and free-speech campaigners – fear that it hands private companies the delicate task of balancing privacy against the public's right to know, and that the powerful will use it to tidy away embarrassing but legitimate stories.
Both concerns have some foundation. The difficulty lies in the fact that the same piece of information can be trivial in one context and vital in another: a decades-old bankruptcy may be irrelevant to a neighbour but highly relevant to someone deciding whether to invest in the person's new company. Any workable principle, therefore, must rest less on the information than on the use to which it is put – a distinction that is far easier to state than to apply.

w: Forgetting now requires less effort

qs.why: “For most of human history, forgetting was the default… The internet has reversed this arrangement.”

qs.a: Asking search engines to remove certain links

qs.why: “ask search engines to remove links… The information itself was not deleted”

items.title: The Consolations of Routine
items.tvi: Niềm an ủi của nếp sống đều đặn
items.text:
Routine has a poor reputation. In the language of self-help it is a rut to be escaped; in fiction it is the grey background against which adventures begin. To describe someone's life as routine is rarely a compliment. Yet many of those whose work we most admire depended on routines of almost monastic strictness. The novelist who wrote for exactly four hours each morning, the composer who walked the same route every afternoon, the scientist who answered letters only on Sundays – such habits recur so often in the biographies of the productive that they can hardly be coincidental.
The explanation may lie in what routine spares us. Every decision, however trivial, demands a little attention. By settling in advance when to work, what to eat and when to sleep, a routine frees that attention for what matters. Far from stifling creativity, it may be its precondition: the mind can wander freely only when the body is on familiar ground.
There is also a quieter consolation. In periods of grief or uncertainty, when larger structures of meaning collapse, routine can offer something to hold on to – the kettle boiled, the dog walked, the bed made. Such acts are trivial, but their regularity asserts that life continues.
None of this is to deny that routines can harden into prisons, or that some disruption is necessary for growth. The art, perhaps, is to treat routine not as a destination but as scaffolding: a structure that supports the building while it is being made, and that can be adjusted, or removed, when it is no longer needed.

items.title: The Burden of the Gift
items.tvi: Gánh nặng của món quà
items.text:
A gift, we are told, is the purest expression of generosity: something given freely, with nothing expected in return. Anthropologists have long found this picture a little naive. In many societies, they observe, a gift creates a bond, and a bond creates an obligation. To accept is to enter a relationship in which one is expected, sooner or later, to reciprocate.
Anyone who has agonised over the price of a present will recognise the mechanism. We calculate, usually without admitting it, what will seem generous without seeming extravagant; too lavish a gift can embarrass the recipient by placing them in debt, while a stingy one may offend. The unspoken arithmetic is rarely discussed, which is perhaps why it works so well.
This is not to say that generosity is a sham. Plenty of people give without keeping accounts, and the pleasure they take in giving is real enough. But it would be a mistake to suppose that sincerity and obligation are mutually exclusive. A birthday present can express genuine affection and, at the same moment, discharge a social duty; the two motives are seldom easy to separate, even for the giver.
It is telling that the most awkward gifts are those that cannot be returned in kind: the favour from a colleague that one has no obvious means of repaying, or the kindness of a stranger in a crisis. Such gifts are welcome, certainly, but they leave a faint discomfort behind, and the temptation to reduce the imbalance as quickly as possible is strong. Gratitude, it seems, is not always a comfortable emotion.

w: It has been disproved by recent research
It is accepted by most societies today
qs.why: “Anthropologists have long found this picture a little naive.”

w: Everyone calculates it in the same way

qs.why: “The unspoken arithmetic is rarely discussed, which is perhaps why it works so well.”

items.title: The Dignity of Ruins
items.tvi: Phẩm giá của những tàn tích
items.text:
Few things attract visitors like a ruin. We travel great distances to stand among broken columns and roofless walls, and we do so with a reverence that we rarely extend to buildings that are merely old. A ruin, it seems, has acquired something that an intact structure lacks: an air of significance earned through loss.
Part of the appeal is surely aesthetic. Time works on stone as a sculptor might, removing the inessential and leaving fragments that invite the imagination to complete them. The eighteenth-century taste for picturesque decay was so strong that wealthy landowners, impatient with nature, sometimes commissioned artificial ruins to adorn their parks. The irony of building a ruin on purpose appears to have troubled few of them.
Yet the fascination is also moral. A ruin reminds us that even the grandest ambitions are provisional; the proud inscription on a toppled monument is a rebuke to anyone inclined to believe that their own age is permanent. Poets have exploited the idea for centuries, and it remains oddly consoling. If empires are subject to erosion, our private failures seem a little less grave.
There is, however, a case for suspicion. Our enjoyment of ruins depends on a certain distance: we admire the crumbling fortress precisely because no one is any longer defending it. Those who live beside such places, and who may be forbidden to alter them in the interests of preservation, sometimes take a less romantic view. Dignity, they might reasonably point out, is easier to attribute to stones than to endure as a neighbour.

qs.a: A sense of importance gained through loss
w: A greater historical accuracy
A more peaceful atmosphere
qs.why: “an air of significance earned through loss.”

qs.q: What attitude does the writer show towards the owners of artificial ruins?
qs.a: Mild amusement at their lack of concern
w: Strong disapproval of their wastefulness
Admiration for their ingenuity
qs.why: “The irony of building a ruin on purpose appears to have troubled few of them.”

qs.q: Why might a ruin be consoling, according to the writer?
qs.a: It suggests that even great powers do not last
w: It proves that old buildings are better made
It encourages people to rebuild
qs.why: “even the grandest ambitions are provisional” … “If empires are subject to erosion, our private failures seem a little less grave.”

qs.q: What is implied about people who live beside ruins?
qs.a: They may find the romantic view hard to share
w: They are usually proud of the site
They are mostly unaware of the site's history
qs.why: “Those who live beside such places… sometimes take a less romantic view.”

items.title: When Proverbs Disagree
items.tvi: Khi các câu tục ngữ mâu thuẫn nhau
items.text:
Proverbs are often credited with the accumulated wisdom of ages, yet a moment's inspection reveals that they cannot all be right. 'Look before you leap,' we are advised; but then, 'he who hesitates is lost.' 'Many hands make light work,' says one saying, while another warns that too many cooks spoil the broth. A cynic might conclude that proverbs are simply a device for justifying whatever one had already decided to do.
That is a little unfair. A proverb is better understood not as a law but as a lens: it picks out a pattern that is true in some circumstances and invites the listener to judge whether those circumstances apply. The advice to be cautious suits the reckless; the advice to be bold suits the timid. What matters is knowing which of them one needs to hear, and no proverb can tell us that.
It is partly for this reason that proverbs survive in speech better than they do in argument. Deployed at the right moment, a well-worn saying lends a remark an air of settled authority and spares the speaker the trouble of explaining. Deployed carelessly, it merely flags the absence of an original thought.
Perhaps the contradictions are, in the end, the most honest thing about them. Human experience is not consistent, and a body of wisdom that pretended otherwise would deserve less trust, not more. We should be wary of anyone who has a proverb for everything, and equally wary of anyone who has none.

qs.q: What does the writer say about the claim that proverbs hold the wisdom of the ages?
qs.a: It is difficult to maintain because proverbs contradict each other
w: It is true only of the oldest proverbs
It is supported by the examples given
qs.why: “a moment's inspection reveals that they cannot all be right.”

qs.q: How does the writer prefer to see a proverb?
qs.a: As a way of looking at a situation
w: As a rule that must be obeyed
As a device for avoiding decisions
qs.why: “A proverb is better understood not as a law but as a lens”

qs.q: What is the writer's attitude towards careless use of proverbs?
qs.a: Critical, because it suggests a lack of original thinking
w: Tolerant, because it makes speech more lively
Amused, because it gives remarks authority
qs.why: “it merely flags the absence of an original thought.”

qs.q: What does the writer conclude about the contradictions between proverbs?
qs.a: They may reflect the real inconsistency of life
w: They show that proverbs should be abandoned
They can be resolved by careful study
qs.why: “Human experience is not consistent”

items.title: The Politics of Naming
items.tvi: Chính trị của việc đặt tên
items.text:
To name a thing is to claim a certain power over it. Parents know this when they agonise over a child's name; cartographers know it when they decide which of two rival names to print on a map. Names are never merely labels. They carry history, allegiance and, not infrequently, an implied argument about who has the right to be there.
Consider how readily a change of name accompanies a change of regime. Streets are renamed after revolutions, and statues come down along with the titles of the people they honoured. Those who object to such changes are often accused of sentimentality, but their grievance is not always trivial. A name is a form of continuity, and to alter it is to suggest that the past it recorded has been officially set aside.
The reverse is also true. Communities that have long been described by outsiders in terms they did not choose sometimes insist on being called by their own word. The request can seem pedantic to those who have used the older term innocently for years. Yet it is hard to deny the logic: if a name is a form of power, then the power to choose it should belong, as far as possible, to the people it describes.
None of this makes the dispute simple. Languages shift, and a word considered respectful in one generation may be thought dated in the next. A sensible person will, I think, accept that there is no final settlement, and will adjust without too much grumbling.

qs.q: What does the writer mean by saying that names are 'never merely labels'?
qs.a: They express claims about history and belonging
w: They are chosen only by those in authority
They change meaning from one language to another
qs.why: “They carry history, allegiance and, not infrequently, an implied argument about who has the right to be there.”

qs.q: Why might people object to renaming streets after a revolution?
qs.a: They feel the past is being officially disregarded
w: They dislike the new names themselves
They believe the old names were more accurate
qs.why: “to alter it is to suggest that the past it recorded has been officially set aside.”

qs.q: What view does the writer take of communities that ask to be called by their own word?
qs.a: The request is logical, though it may seem fussy to some
w: The request is justified only if the old term was offensive
The request is likely to be ignored by most people
qs.why: “it is hard to deny the logic”

qs.q: What is the writer's attitude in the final paragraph?
qs.a: Relaxed, accepting that usage will keep changing
w: Frustrated by the instability of language
Insistent that one settlement is needed
qs.why: “will adjust without too much grumbling.”

items.title: In Defence of the Amateur
items.tvi: Bênh vực người nghiệp dư
items.text:
The word 'amateur' has fallen on hard times. In everyday speech it has become almost an insult, a synonym for the clumsy and the half-informed. This is a curious fate for a term that originally meant simply one who does something for love. The amateur astronomer, the weekend naturalist and the village historian have, in their time, contributed observations that professionals had neither the leisure nor the inclination to collect.
There is something to be said for the amateur's position. Freed from the need to publish, to secure funding or to impress a committee, he or she can follow a curiosity wherever it leads, including into territory that careful careers avoid. Professionals, by contrast, are trained to defend a field, and the habits that make them reliable can also make them reluctant to question its assumptions.
It would be foolish, however, to romanticise the matter. Enthusiasm is not expertise, and the history of science is cluttered with confident outsiders who were simply wrong. The usual outcome, if one is honest, is that the amateur's theory dissolves on contact with the evidence, and one hopes the person is gracious about it.
What the amateur offers, then, is less a rival to professional knowledge than a reminder of its purpose. Knowledge that is pursued only as a means of earning a living can lose touch with the delight that prompted the inquiry in the first place. A society that wishes to keep that delight alive could do worse than to encourage those who pursue it unpaid.

qs.q: What does the writer say about the original meaning of 'amateur'?
qs.a: It referred to someone motivated by love of the activity
w: It described a person without any training
It was always used in a mildly critical way
qs.why: “a term that originally meant simply one who does something for love.”

qs.q: What advantage does the writer identify for amateurs?
qs.a: They can pursue ideas without institutional pressures
w: They are less likely to make mistakes
They usually have better equipment than professionals
qs.why: “Freed from the need to publish, to secure funding or to impress a committee”

qs.q: What can be inferred from the phrase 'one hopes the person is gracious about it'?
qs.a: Amateurs whose ideas fail do not always accept it well
w: Most amateur theories turn out to be correct
Professionals are usually kind to amateurs
qs.why: “the amateur's theory dissolves on contact with the evidence, and one hopes the person is gracious about it.”

qs.q: What is the writer's main conclusion?
qs.a: Amateurs keep alive the pleasure that drives learning
w: Amateurs should replace professionals in some fields
Professional knowledge has lost its value
qs.why: “Knowledge that is pursued only as a means of earning a living can lose touch with the delight that prompted the inquiry”

items.title: The Art of Being Wrong
items.tvi: Nghệ thuật nhận mình sai
items.text:
Admitting an error in public is widely held to be a mark of integrity, and just as widely avoided. The reasons are not hard to find. In most professions a retraction is read as weakness, and a person who changes their mind may be accused of inconsistency by the very people who once demanded open-mindedness. It is a peculiar arrangement: we praise those who revise their views and punish them for doing so.
Part of the difficulty lies in how we imagine confidence. We tend to treat certainty as evidence of competence, so that the speaker who hedges is judged less capable than the one who does not. Yet anyone who has watched an expert at work knows that real mastery usually comes with a lively sense of what one does not know. The loudest assurance is often the least reliable.
There is also the matter of timing. A mistake corrected quickly and without fuss tends to be forgiven; one defended for years, at increasing cost, is remembered. The instinct to protect one's earlier position by digging in is natural, but it converts an ordinary error into something much harder to excuse.
If institutions wished to encourage honesty, they might begin by making it cheaper. A culture in which saying 'I was mistaken' brought no penalty beyond a moment's discomfort would surely produce better decisions than one in which every error must be hidden. Individuals can help by setting an example, though few, one suspects, will volunteer to be first.

qs.q: What contradiction does the writer point out in the first paragraph?
qs.a: Open-mindedness is admired but then penalised
w: Experts avoid admitting mistakes while amateurs do not
Retractions are praised only when they are public
qs.why: “we praise those who revise their views and punish them for doing so.”

qs.q: What does the writer suggest about people who speak with great certainty?
qs.a: Their confidence may be a poor guide to their reliability
w: They are usually the most skilled experts
They tend to correct their errors quickly
qs.why: “The loudest assurance is often the least reliable.”

qs.q: According to the writer, why does defending an error for years make matters worse?
qs.a: It turns a minor mistake into a serious fault
w: It makes the original mistake harder to remember
It shows that the person is under pressure
qs.why: “it converts an ordinary error into something much harder to excuse.”

qs.q: What attitude does the writer express in the last sentence?
qs.a: Doubt that many people will take the lead
w: Confidence that individuals will change quickly
Disapproval of those who set an example
qs.why: “few, one suspects, will volunteer to be first.”

items.title: What the Archive Cannot Say
items.tvi: Điều mà kho lưu trữ không nói được
items.text:
An archive carries an air of authority. Rows of boxes, each neatly labelled, suggest that the past has been kept in good order and that anyone who consults it will find the truth waiting. Historians know better. Every archive is the product of decisions: someone chose what to keep, someone else what to discard, and a great deal was simply never written down in the first place.
Consider whose lives are likely to leave records. Governments and wealthy families document themselves lavishly; farm workers, servants and the poor appear mostly when they come into contact with the law or with charity. The historian who wishes to hear their voices must work with fragments, such as a line in a court register or a name on a ship's list, and must resist the temptation to fill the gaps with confident invention.
Silence in the record can therefore be misleading. It is easy to assume that what is not mentioned did not happen, or did not matter. But absence is often a sign of how little those in charge cared to note, not of how little there was to note.
This does not make the archive worthless. On the contrary, a careful reader can learn a good deal from what has been omitted, just as a detective learns from the dog that did not bark. The discipline lies in asking, of every document, not only what it says but who bothered to write it, and who did not.

qs.q: What does the writer say historians understand about archives?
qs.a: They reflect choices about what to keep and what to lose
w: They are mostly organised by social class
They contain every important document
qs.why: “Every archive is the product of decisions”

qs.q: According to the writer, when do poor people usually appear in records?
qs.a: When they deal with the law or charities
w: When they work for wealthy families
When they travel abroad
qs.why: “appear mostly when they come into contact with the law or with charity.”

qs.q: What does the writer imply about gaps in the record?
qs.a: They may show what the authorities did not think worth recording
w: They prove that nothing important took place
They are usually caused by accidental damage
qs.why: “absence is often a sign of how little those in charge cared to note”

qs.q: What is the point of the reference to 'the dog that did not bark'?
qs.a: Omissions can themselves be informative
w: Detectives make better historians
Records are often deliberately misleading
qs.why: “a careful reader can learn a good deal from what has been omitted, just as a detective learns from the dog that did not bark.”

items.title: The Case for Slow Reading
items.tvi: Lập luận cho việc đọc chậm
items.text:
We have grown accustomed to reading at speed. Faced with an endless supply of articles, messages and reports, we skim, scan and search for the relevant paragraph, and we congratulate ourselves on how much we have 'covered'. There is nothing wrong with this for the purposes of information. The difficulty arises when we apply the same habit to writing that was never meant to be consumed quickly.
A dense argument or a carefully made poem rewards attention in proportion to the time it receives. Sentences are built to be turned over; an image may reveal its point only on a second or third meeting. The reader in a hurry notices what is obvious and misses the rest, and then, rather unfairly, concludes that the work was not much good.
Slow reading is not the same as slow thinking, still less a pious exercise in self-improvement. It simply means letting a text set its own pace, rereading a difficult passage without resentment and pausing to notice why a particular word was chosen. Those who do so often report that the experience resembles conversation more than consumption.
Of course, no one can read everything slowly, and it would be absurd to try. The skill is one of selection: deciding which few books deserve the effort and giving them the hours they ask for. It is a modest proposal, but in an age that measures reading by volume, it has acquired something of the force of an act of resistance.

qs.a: It suits information but not all writing
w: It should be avoided in all situations
It is the best way to understand an argument
qs.why: “There is nothing wrong with this for the purposes of information. The difficulty arises when we apply the same habit to writing that was never meant to be consumed quickly.”

qs.a: They miss much of it, then blame the work
w: They read it in the wrong order
They are unfamiliar with poetic vocabulary
qs.why: “The reader in a hurry notices what is obvious and misses the rest, and then, rather unfairly, concludes that the work was not much good.”

qs.a: As letting the text decide the speed
w: As a way of improving one's character
As thinking more slowly than usual
qs.why: “letting a text set its own pace”

It is a recent idea in education

items.title: Luxury and the Value of Scarcity
items.tvi: Xa xỉ và giá trị của sự khan hiếm
items.text:
Economists like to say that price reflects scarcity, and for most goods this is a sufficient explanation. Luxury, however, behaves rather oddly. A handbag that costs a hundred times more than a perfectly sound alternative is not a hundred times more useful, and those who buy it are seldom under that illusion. What they are buying is something else: a signal.
The signal works only if it is difficult to imitate. A product that anyone could afford would cease to say anything about its owner, which is why prestigious makers go to remarkable lengths to remain exclusive. Waiting lists are lengthened, production is limited and discounts are refused. The shortage is, in part, manufactured, and its manufacture is the whole point of the exercise.
It would be easy to dismiss all this as vanity, but that is perhaps too simple. People have always used objects to express belonging and aspiration, and the craftsmen who make the finest goods often take great pride in the work. Whether the result is worth the price is a question of taste; that it is worth something to somebody is evident from the sales figures.
What remains slightly puzzling is how quickly the idea of luxury moves. Items that once symbolised rare privilege, such as spices or sugar, are now unremarkable, while experiences and time have taken their place. One suspects that whatever is currently thought scarce will be tomorrow's commonplace, and that the industry will simply find something else to withhold.

qs.q: What does the writer suggest about people who buy expensive handbags?
qs.a: They know it offers little extra practical value
w: They mistakenly believe it is much better made
They buy it mainly as a long-term investment
qs.why: “those who buy it are seldom under that illusion.”

qs.q: Why do prestigious makers limit their output?
qs.a: Exclusivity is what gives the product its meaning
w: They cannot find enough skilled craftsmen
They wish to keep prices low for loyal customers
qs.why: “The shortage is, in part, manufactured, and its manufacture is the whole point of the exercise.”

qs.q: What is the writer's attitude towards luxury goods?
qs.a: Not entirely dismissive, though somewhat sceptical
w: Openly hostile to those who buy them
Enthusiastic about their craftsmanship
qs.why: “It would be easy to dismiss all this as vanity, but that is perhaps too simple.”

qs.q: What does the final sentence imply about the luxury industry?
qs.a: It will keep adapting to what people regard as rare
w: It will eventually lose its customers
It will move away from exclusive products
qs.why: “the industry will simply find something else to withhold.”
